description: Impacts of hosting a major event during the event itself, and the long-term legacy — good and bad.
content_html:
Impacts During the Event

Once a major sporting event begins, its effects on the host city and nation are immediate and highly visible. Some are clearly positive; others are disruptive or costly. Understanding both sides is essential for evaluation questions, which are common on this topic.

Key Fact

During-event positives include increased tourism and spending, short-term employment, improved national morale, raised international profile and media coverage. Negatives include disruption from transport congestion, noise and litter, security costs, terrorism risk, and in some cases displacement of local residents from areas around venues.

Positive Impacts During the Event

Tourism and economic activity peak during a major event. Spectators travelling from overseas spend money on hotels, food, transport and retail. The 2024 Paris Games attracted millions of visitors, delivering a significant boost to the French economy during a competitive summer tourism season. Short-term employment surges: catering staff, security guards, stewards, translators, media crew and volunteers are all needed in large numbers.

National morale and social cohesion are harder to measure but often cited as major positives. A home nation athlete winning a medal, or simply sharing the experience of watching elite sport together, generates a collective sense of pride. The 2024 Paris Olympics opening ceremony — held along the River Seine — was widely reported as a moment of national celebration. International profile rises sharply: the host nation’s culture, landmarks and people are broadcast to a global audience. This can increase inbound tourism in the months and years that follow.

Not all residents welcome a major event on their doorstep. Transport congestion affects local commuters when roads and public transport are saturated with visitors. Noise, litter, and crowds in residential neighbourhoods disrupt ordinary daily life. Security costs are substantial: the Paris 2024 Games deployed 45,000 security personnel and involved NATO partner support, at a cost running into hundreds of millions of euros. Terrorism risk is a genuine concern for organisers — every modern major event requires detailed counter-terrorism planning. Ironically, the “touristification” effect can drive up local prices, pushing everyday goods and accommodation beyond the reach of residents who live near venues.

What Is Legacy?

Legacy refers to the lasting impact of a major event after the final medal ceremony. Legacy questions are a favourite in extended-response questions because they demand evaluation — candidates must weigh positives against negatives and reach a reasoned judgement. A strong legacy answer will always address both sides and often pivot on a specific case study to ground the argument.

Positive Legacy: London 2012

The 2012 London Olympics is frequently cited as a model of positive legacy. The Olympic Park in Stratford, east London, was built on a heavily polluted former industrial site. After the Games, it was transformed into the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park — a public green space with world-class sporting venues (the London Stadium, Aquatics Centre, Velodrome), new homes, and a revitalised neighbourhood in one of London’s most deprived boroughs. Transport investment including the Docklands Light Railway extension and upgraded rail links served the area long after the event. Participation in cycling notably increased following Team GB’s remarkable haul of medals in the velodrome, which inspired a generation — though critics note that funding cuts to grassroots sport in subsequent years undermined some of these participation gains.

Key Fact

London 2012’s legacy includes the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park (regenerated deprived area of east London), the Aquatics Centre and Velodrome (still in public use), improved transport infrastructure, and a documented increase in cycling participation. However, grassroots sport funding was later cut, limiting long-term participation gains.

Negative Legacy: The “White Elephant” Problem

Not every host city achieves London’s outcomes. White elephants are venues built for events that serve no sustainable purpose once the competition is over. The Athens 2004 Olympics is the most cited cautionary example: within a decade of the Games, most of the venues built specifically for the event had fallen into disrepair or sat empty. Greece’s financial crisis made maintaining expensive facilities impossible, and the sites became symbols of over-investment. The estimated cost of the Athens Games was around £7–9 billion, much of which is judged to have delivered no lasting benefit.

The cost vs revenue question is central to any legacy evaluation. Host cities typically spend far more than they earn from ticket sales, broadcasting rights and tourism. The gap is funded by taxpayers. When the promised regeneration, tourism boost or participation increase fails to materialise, the event is retrospectively judged as a financial burden rather than a national asset. Displacement without return is a related legacy concern: communities uprooted before an event do not always benefit from any regeneration that follows.

Paris 2024 attempted to learn from previous Games by deliberately avoiding purpose-built “white elephant” venues where possible. Many events used existing or temporary structures — beach volleyball at the Trocadéro, equestrian events at Versailles, athletics at the Stade de France. The ambition was that no new permanent venue would be left unused after the Games. The swimming of the marathon open-water race and triathlon in the River Seine was a deliberate legacy signal: the city invested in cleaning the Seine to a standard that would benefit Parisian residents after the Games (the river had been closed to swimming for 100 years). Whether these ambitions translate into real long-term community benefit will take years to assess.

Evaluating Legacy

Evaluating legacy requires looking at multiple dimensions: improved sporting facilities and whether local communities can access them; participation rates in the host nation’s sport; transport infrastructure improvements; international profile and its effect on tourism; and the financial balance between what was spent and what was gained. A high-quality evaluation does not simply list these dimensions — it argues which factors matter most in the specific context of the question, and draws a clear concluding judgement.
exam_tip_html: Legacy questions almost always use the ‘evaluate’ command word, which means you must give a balanced argument and reach a clear conclusion. The most common examiner feedback on this topic is: (1) students gave only positives or only negatives; (2) students made a conclusion but did not justify it with their strongest point; (3) answers were generic — not applied to a named case study. Always name at least one event (London 2012 and Athens 2004 make an ideal contrasting pair) and use it to anchor your points. A conclusion like “the legacy depends on how thoroughly the host city plans for reuse of facilities before the event begins” is far stronger than simply “London 2012 was good”.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • During-event positives include tourism, short-term jobs, national morale and international profile. Negatives include congestion, security costs, local disruption and price rises for residents.
  • Legacy is the long-term impact of a major event. London 2012 is the positive model (Olympic Park, transport, participation). Athens 2004 is the cautionary tale (white elephant venues, financial overreach).
  • A strong evaluation of legacy considers facilities reuse, participation, infrastructure, international profile, and cost vs revenue — and reaches a justified conclusion about which factors matter most.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a 'white elephant' in the context of major sporting events?
A) A venue that is sold to a private owner after the event for use as a concert hall
B) A stadium built for the Olympics that becomes a permanent home ground for a local football club
C) A purpose-built velodrome that is left empty and deteriorating after the Games
D) A temporary beach volleyball court dismantled after the event as planned
practice_questions.marks: C) A purpose-built velodrome that is left empty and deteriorating after the Games [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two positive impacts that occur during a major sporting event for the host city.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per distinct positive (maximum 2 marks). Acceptable answers:
- Increased tourism and visitor spending
- Short-term job creation (catering, security, stewarding, media)
- Boost to national morale / social cohesion
- Raised international profile / global media coverage
- Increased interest in and coverage of sport
Do not award a second mark for the same point described differently.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by 'legacy' in the context of hosting a major sporting event.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
- 1 mark: correct definition — the lasting, long-term effects that remain after a major sporting event has ended
- 1 mark: identification of an area of legacy (e.g. sporting facilities, transport infrastructure, participation rates, international reputation, financial impact)
- 1 mark: applied example (e.g. Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park remaining in use after London 2012; Athens 2004 venues falling into disrepair; Paris 2024 Seine-cleaning project benefiting Parisians)
A definition alone with no development earns 1 mark maximum.

practice_questions.text: Describe two negative legacies that can result from hosting the Olympic Games. Use examples from specific host cities to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks. Credit two distinct negative legacies with development:
- White elephant venues: purpose-built facilities that fall into disuse, as seen most starkly in Athens 2004 where most venues were abandoned within a decade.
- Financial burden: costs far exceeded revenue. Athens 2004 estimated at around £7-9bn, contributing to Greece's later fiscal crisis.
- Displacement without return: communities moved to make way for venues who do not benefit from post-event regeneration.
- Debt and austerity: host nation government may face years of debt repayment, diverting public funds from health, education or welfare.
Named example required for top marks. An answer with no named host city is capped at 2 marks.

practice_questions.text:
Riverton City is a medium-sized UK city that hosted a major athletics world championship three years ago. The new 50,000-seat athletics stadium is now used only for occasional concerts, and local athletics participation has not increased.

Evaluate whether the legacy of hosting a major sporting event is likely to be positive or negative for a host city like Riverton.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Sophisticated, balanced evaluation that addresses multiple dimensions of legacy (facilities, participation, economic, infrastructure, international profile). Arguments are developed beyond assertion. A named or applied example (London 2012, Athens 2004, or the Riverton scenario itself) is used to anchor points. A clear, justified conclusion is reached that links back to the question — e.g. 'legacy is likely to be positive only when reuse planning is embedded in the original bid, as London 2012 demonstrated; without this, white elephant and debt risks dominate as in Athens 2004.' Riverton scenario is engaged with meaningfully.

Secure (5-6 marks): Clear argument on both sides, at least two developed points in each direction. A conclusion is present but may not be fully substantiated. Named example likely present.

Developing (3-4 marks): Some argument on both sides, but development is limited and may be list-like. Conclusion present but underdeveloped. Named example may be absent.

Emerging (1-2 marks): One-sided or very thin answer. Little engagement with the question's specific context. No real evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Identify one positive impact on national morale during a major sporting event, and explain why this impact may not last once the event is over.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
- 1 mark: identify a positive morale impact (e.g. shared national pride in host nation's athletes winning medals; collective watching experience; sense of unity and celebration)
- 1 mark: explain why it may not last (morale is temporary / tied to event itself; once coverage ends, everyday social divisions and issues return; participation gains may not follow morale boosts if funding is not sustained)
- 1 mark: apply or develop (e.g. Team GB cycling medals at London 2012 boosted cycling interest but grassroots funding was later cut, limiting long-term participation growth)

knowledge_checks.q: Which term describes a venue built for a major event that becomes unused or deteriorates afterwards?
Which Olympic Games is most frequently cited as a cautionary tale for white elephant venues and financial overreach?
The Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park in Stratford, east London, is a positive example of _____ from the 2012 Games.
_____ refers to the long-term effects — positive or negative — that remain after a major sporting event has ended.
Match each during/legacy impact to the correct category (positive or negative).
left: Increased tourism and visitor spending during the event
Purpose-built venues falling into disrepair after the event

flashcard_questions.q: What is 'legacy' in the context of a major sporting event?
flashcard_questions.a: The long-term positive or negative effects that remain after the event has ended.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a 'white elephant' in the context of hosting major events?
flashcard_questions.a: A venue built for an event that becomes unused or too expensive to maintain afterwards.

flashcard_questions.q: Which Olympic host city is most often cited as the cautionary 'white elephant' example?
flashcard_questions.a: Athens 2004, where most venues fell into disrepair within a decade.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two specific positive legacy outcomes from the London 2012 Olympics.
flashcard_questions.a: Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park (east London regeneration) and improved transport infrastructure.

flashcard_questions.q: Which area of London was regenerated as a direct result of the 2012 Olympic Games?
flashcard_questions.a: Stratford, in the London Borough of Newham.

flashcard_questions.q: How did Paris 2024 attempt to avoid white elephant venues?
flashcard_questions.a: By using existing or temporary structures rather than building new permanent venues where possible.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two positive impacts that happen during a major sporting event.
What does 'displacement without return' mean as a legacy concern?
flashcard_questions.a: Communities moved to make way for venues who receive no benefit from post-event regeneration.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two dimensions a student should cover when evaluating the legacy of a major event.
flashcard_questions.a: Facilities reuse and participation rates. (Also accept: transport, international profile, cost vs revenue.)

flashcard_questions.q: Why is national morale during an event considered a temporary rather than lasting legacy?
flashcard_questions.a: Once the event ends, coverage stops and everyday social divisions and funding challenges return.

flashcard_questions.q: The Paris 2024 organising committee cleaned the River Seine primarily as what kind of legacy investment?
flashcard_questions.a: Allowing Parisians to swim in the Seine again after 100 years of it being closed to public use.

glossary_terms.definition: The long-term effects — positive or negative — that remain after a major sporting event has ended, including changes to facilities, infrastructure, participation, economy and international reputation.
A costly facility or infrastructure project that is built for a major event but becomes unused, under-used or prohibitively expensive to maintain afterwards.
A situation where residents are forced out of an area — often to make way for event venues — and are unable to return or participate in any community benefit once the event is over.
